detailed_rationale:
Jyothy Labs is a mid-sized Indian FMCG company built around fabric care (Ujala fabric whitener, reportedly ~84% category share, plus Henko/Mr. White/Morelight detergents), dishwashing (Pril, Exo), household insecticides, and a smaller personal-care portfolio. The company is almost debt-free and generates healthy returns on capital (ROCE ~24.6%, ROE ~19% in the latest full year), with a consistent 35-38% dividend payout.

The growth picture, however, is genuinely weak and has been for several quarters: FY2025 full-year sales grew only ~3% with net profit essentially flat (0% YoY), and the TTM sales growth rate is just ~3% against a slower-decelerating 3-year CAGR of ~9% and 5-year CAGR of ~11% -- a clear deceleration trend, not a one-off dip. Working capital days have also risen from 29 to 45, a real (if moderate) deterioration in cash-conversion efficiency worth watching. The stock price has fallen sharply (roughly -40% over one year, -15% over three years per public data), which has brought the PE down to a reasonable ~19-20x -- cheap by FMCG standards -- but that de-rating is itself a rational market response to the growth stall rather than a mispricing to be relied upon as an automatic value signal. Fabric care and dishwashing are largely mature, highly competitive categories (contesting with Hindustan Unilever, P&G and increasingly private labels), which structurally caps volume growth absent genuine premiumization or new-category success in personal care.
recommendation_rationale: The quant score is a genuine Sell (1y recommendation Sell, composite driven by weak growth), and our research does not surface a rescue case: the growth weakness (TTM sales +3%, profit flat) and working-capital deterioration look like real, structural category maturity issues rather than a one-off, data-quality, or misclassification problem that would justify overriding to Hold. Quality metrics (ROE, ROCE, low leverage) are genuinely good, but under this framework growth is the swing factor, and growth here is honestly weak -- so we keep the quant Sell rather than force a rescue.
summary: Jyothy Labs is a financially conservative, well-run FMCG company (Ujala, Henko, Pril, Exo) with strong returns on capital and almost no debt, but its growth has stalled -- sales grew only about 3% in the latest full year with profit essentially flat, and working capital efficiency has slipped. The stock has already fallen sharply and now trades at a reasonable valuation, but we do not see a clear catalyst to reaccelerate growth in a mature, competitive category, so we maintain the model's Sell call.
positive_para: The company is financially conservative and profitable -- almost debt-free, with ROCE near 25% and a consistent dividend payout -- and it holds a dominant position in the niche fabric-whitener category through the Ujala brand. The sharp share-price decline has brought valuation down to a reasonable ~19-20x earnings, cheap relative to FMCG peers, which limits further valuation-driven downside if growth merely stabilizes rather than reaccelerates.
negative_para: Growth has genuinely stalled: full-year sales grew only ~3% with profit flat, and the growth rate has been decelerating across the 5-year, 3-year and TTM windows rather than showing any sign of an inflection. Working capital days have risen from 29 to 45, a real (if not yet alarming) deterioration in cash conversion. The core categories -- fabric care and dishwashing -- are mature and intensely competitive against much larger multinational rivals, leaving limited room for volume-led re-acceleration without a genuine new growth driver (e.g., successful personal-care expansion), which has not yet shown up meaningfully in the numbers.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At ~19-20x earnings the market is now pricing Jyothy Labs closer to a low-single-digit structural grower, which is roughly consistent with the delivered numbers (TTM sales growth ~3%, profit flat) -- so the stock looks fairly valued for what it is currently delivering, not obviously cheap, since there is no clear evidence yet of the growth reacceleration that would be needed to justify paying up further.
